You are an information-extraction assistant for ESG sustainability reports.

You will be given:
- A KPI to extract.
- The list of acceptable units for that KPI.
- Passages of text from a corporate sustainability report.

Your job: return the KPI's MOST RECENT year value by calling the `record_kpi` tool.

Rules:
- If the document shows multiple year columns (e.g. "2021 2022 2023 2024 2025"), pick the LATEST year's value.
- Pick the CONSOLIDATED / TOTAL group-level value — not a subsidiary, business segment, or sub-component breakdown.
- Pick the ABSOLUTE total — not an intensity ratio (e.g. tCO2e/$, MWh/€, l/kWh) or a percentage.
- For Scope 1 emissions: pick "Total gross Scope 1 GHG emissions" / "Scope 1 (direct) greenhouse gas emissions". If the report distinguishes "consolidated" from "operational control + non-consolidated entities" (ESRS-aligned reporting, common in Shell/Eni), pick the LARGER ESRS-aligned figure that includes operated non-consolidated entities, not the consolidated-only sub-total. Never pick Scope 2, Scope 3, methane-only, intensity, or net (Scope 1+2 combined).
- For total energy consumption: pick the company-wide total energy CONSUMED — not energy produced from renewables, fuel-only, or electricity-only sub-totals. If the report distinguishes "operational control" from "ESRS-aligned + non-consolidated", pick the LARGER ESRS-aligned figure.
- For water consumption: ONLY pick a value labelled "water CONSUMPTION" or "freshwater CONSUMPTION" or "net water consumption". REJECT every value labelled "withdrawal", "withdrawn", "discharge", "discharged", "recycled", "reclaimed", "reused", "produced water", or "wastewater". This rule is STRICT — when in doubt between consumption and withdrawal, return null. If the report distinguishes an "operational control" boundary from a "financial control" (or "ESRS") boundary for water (common in Shell), prefer the OPERATIONAL CONTROL figure — that is the primary disclosure for water in oil & gas reports, and the financial-control table is a supplementary view.
- Multiply out magnitude prefixes yourself: if the document says "82.0 million m³" return value=82000000, unit=m3. If it says "32,141 thousand m³" return value=32141000, unit=m3. If it says "168.59 TWh" you may either return value=168.59, unit=TWh OR multiply out — but NEVER write a unit that contains a magnitude word (e.g. never "million m3", "thousand m3", "Mm3", "million cubic metres"). The unit MUST be a single base unit from the listed acceptable units.
- If the KPI is not reported clearly in this passage, call the tool with value=null, unit=null.
- Never guess or infer from breakdowns if there is no consolidated total — use value=null.
- `reporting_year` is the year the value refers to (the most recent column).
- `source_snippet` is the exact quoted text supporting the value (max 200 chars).

## Methodological Note

## Scope 1-2

In line with applicable regulatory requirements and consistent with major international standards (WBCSD/WRI GHG Protocol Initiative Standard and sector best practices), GHG emissions are reported for all relevant emission sources, considering the following gases: CO 2 , CH 4 and N 2 O. Other greenhouse gases (HFCs, PFCs, SF 6 , NF 3 ), based on analysis of available data and in line with Oil & Gas sector practice, are not considered significant as they account for approximately 0.02% of total GHG emissions. Global Warming Potentials (GWPs) from the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) over a 100-year horizon are used for conversion into CO2eq.: 29.8 for CH 4 and 273 for N 2 O. Scope 1 GHG emissions are classified into the following categories: (i) Combustion and process (stationary combustion, mobile sources and industrial-process operations); (ii) Flaring (controlled combustion of hydrocarbons via flare); (iii) Venting (controlled release to the atmosphere of unburned gas, mainly CH 4 ,  during operational activities such as Oil & Gas exploration and production, power generation and gas transportation); (iv) Fugitive emissions (unintentional methane leaks from equipment and components such as pumps, valves, compressor seals, etc.). Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions are calculated based on measurement or, where not available, estimation (e.g., fuel consumed, electricity purchased, distance travelled). Depending on their physical origin, data are sourced from: (i) fuel-meter readings; (ii) utility bills (e.g., electricity consumption); (iii) direct measurement (e.g., LDAR campaigns for fugitive emissions); (iv) other methods applied at specific Eni sites and facilities. Emission factors are determined based on gas chemical composition or derived from literature sources. Specifically: (i) for installations subject to the EU ETS, national standard parameters under Regulation (EU) 2018/2066 (updated for 2025) issued by the Ministry for Ecological Transition are applied for natural gas, LPG, refinery fuel gas, petroleum-derived gas and flare gas; (ii) for other installations, the main references are the IPCC guidelines and the API Compendium of Greenhouse Gas Emissions Methodologies for the Oil and Natural Gas Industry (2009/2021) for CO 2 , CH 4 and N 2 O. At Eni sites where LDAR programmes are in place, fugitive CH 4 emissions are determined using periodic leak-measurement campaigns. Measurement results are used to quantify annual emissions by applying emission factors from API, EPA (e.g., EPA Protocol No. 453) and OGMP standards. At sites where LDAR is not implemented, fugitive emissions are estimated based on equipment-component inventories (valves, flanges, etc.) or on oil and gas production volumes, using standard emission factors (API Compendium). Biogenic CO 2 Scope 1 emissions are reported separately; they amounted to 0.27 and 0.21 MtCO2eq. in 2024 and 2025 respectively, and derive from biomass combustion and biomethane production processes. Scope 2 emissions are reported according to two approaches: a)  Location-Based - based on the average electricity-generation mix of the Country from which third-party electricity is purchased (IEA Emission Factors database); b) Market-Based - based on supplier-specific electricity-data, considering the share of renewable electricity, the Country residual mix, and contractual instruments linked or unlinked to the supply contracts (in 2025, these instruments covered around 55% of total electricity purchases). Emissions associated with non-renewable or non-certified supply are calculated using supplier-specific factors or the residual mix where available; otherwise, the Country electricity mix is used (AIB 2024 factors). Emission factors for steam purchases are derived from the API Compendium. Biogenic CO 2 Scope 2 emissions are not estimated as they are deemed not significant. ## SCENARIO ANALYSIS

The identification of Eni's physical and transition risks is also supported by an in-depth analysis of climate scenarios. At the international level, a wide range of scenarios currently exists, developed by numerous analysts, consultants, organisations and energy-sector entities. These scenarios rely on different construction methodologies and outline a broad spectrum of possible evolutions of the energy system. They combine decarbonisation levers, technologies, assumptions on the evolution of consumption patterns and policy frameworks in different ways, in order to illustrate potential future trajectories and provide a useful reference framework for guiding strategic choices and policy directions. In this context, given the absence of universally recognised decarbonisation pathways for the Oil & Gas sector, Eni  analyses multiple prospective pathways characterised by heterogeneous mixes of solutions and milestones, among which those developed by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) are particularly relevant. Specifically, climate scenarios belonging to the IPCC C1-C2 categories were used as a reference for assessing the compatibility of Eni decarbonisation plan 25  with trajectories aligned with the 1.5°C limit by 2100, while acknowledging the intrinsic limitations of comparing a corporate context with the global one (see Decarbonisation levers ). The IEA Net Zero Emissions (NZE) scenario was considered for assessing the resilience of Eni's strategy to transition risks (see Resilience of the strategy to transition scenarios ), whereas the IPCC SSP5-RCP8.5 (C8) scenario was used for the analysis of physical risks (see Physical risks ).

## Main reference scenarios

IEA - Net Zero Emissions (NZE) Scenario: in the World Energy Outlook 2025, the IEA revised the assumptions underpinning the NZE scenario (the scenario targeting Net Zero emissions by 2050), shifting from a limited-overshoot pathway to a high-overshoot 26  one. In this scenario - for which the IEA provides numerical detail only at the global level - decarbonisation of the energy system is achieved primarily through increasing electrification and a major scale-up of variable renewables (whose share in the power-generation mix rises from today's 15% to around 75% in 2050), improved energy efficiency, and rapid deployment of CO 2 capture and storage technologies for industrial processes (CCUS), bioenergy with CCS (BECCS) and direct air capture (DACS). In terms of energy mix, the NZE-IEA scenario features a substantial decline in the role of fossil fuels, whose share in the global mix drops from the current 79% to 16% by 2050, alongside a falling energy demand (0.5% per year on average between 2024 and 2050). By 2050, the most affected energy source is coal, with emissions falling by 99% compared with 2024 (consumption down 92%), followed by natural gas (95% emissions; consumption down 80%) and oil (90% emissions; consumption down 77%).

Unlike the IEA, the IPCC develops climate scenarios 27  by considering all GHG emissions, not only CO 2 from the energy sector. These scenarios are grouped into eight categories (C1-C8) 28  based on the projected increase in global temperature by 2100 associated with each pathway. The decarbonisation levers and technologies deployed in these pathways, while broadly similar to those of the NZE-IEA scenario, are combined in different ways.
